prompt: Compared with other commercial vehicles, how stable are doubles and triples?
choices: They are more stable because the weight is spread out
They are more stable when empty than loaded
They are about as stable as a straight truck
They are less stable
explanation: Doubles and triples are less stable than other commercial vehicles, and more things can go wrong when pulling two or three trailers.

prompt: To keep a set of doubles from rolling over, you should:
choices: Brake hard just before each curve, then speed up in it
Steer gently and go slowly around corners, ramps and curves
Keep the heavier trailer at the rear of the set
Take curves at the posted speed for trucks
explanation: Preventing rollover means steering gently and going slowly around corners, on-ramps, off-ramps and curves.

prompt: A speed that is safe on a curve for a single-trailer rig is:
choices: Possibly too fast for a set of doubles or triples
Always safe for doubles if the trailers are empty
Safe for doubles as long as you stay in your lane
Too slow for doubles, which track better on curves
explanation: A safe curve speed for a straight truck or single-trailer combination may be too fast for doubles or triples, which roll over more easily.

prompt: In a doubles or triples combination, which unit is most likely to turn over?
choices: The tractor
The converter dolly
The last trailer
The first trailer
explanation: Because of the crack-the-whip effect, the last trailer in a combination is the one most likely to turn over.

prompt: Doubles and triples are more likely to turn over than other combination vehicles mainly because of:
choices: Weaker fifth wheels
The crack-the-whip effect
Air brake lag on the tractor
Their higher engine power
explanation: The crack-the-whip effect makes doubles and triples more likely to turn over than other combination vehicles, so you must steer gently.

prompt: What causes the crack-the-whip effect in combination vehicles?
choices: Off-tracking on tight turns
Brake fade on the trailers
Rearward amplification
Liquid surge in the cargo
explanation: Rearward amplification causes the crack-the-whip effect: a quick steering movement grows larger toward the rear of the rig.

prompt: Triples have a rearward amplification of about 3.5. What does that mean?
choices: You must drive 3.5 mph slower on curves than you would with doubles
The last trailer swings 3.5 feet wider than the first trailer in turns
The rig needs 3.5 times the stopping distance of a five-axle tractor
The last trailer rolls over 3.5 times as easily as a five-axle tractor
explanation: A rearward amplification of 3.5 means you can roll the last trailer of a triples rig 3.5 times as easily as a five-axle tractor.

prompt: Which maneuver is most likely to trigger a crack-the-whip rollover of a rear trailer?
choices: A quick lane change
A slow, gradual lane change
Gentle braking on a straight road
Downshifting before a hill
explanation: A quick lane change can create the crack-the-whip effect and turn the rear trailer over. Many crashes involve only the trailer overturning.

prompt: Why should you look far ahead when pulling doubles or triples?
choices: So you can use the full width of the road on curves
So you can slow down or change lanes gradually
So you can pass other vehicles more often
So you can delay braking until the last moment
explanation: Doubles and triples must be driven very smoothly to avoid rollover or jackknife, so look far ahead to make gradual changes.

prompt: Why do doubles and triples need more space than other commercial vehicles?
choices: They are longer and cannot be turned or stopped suddenly
Their trailers have no brakes of their own
They are wider than other trailers
They must keep to the left lane
explanation: Doubles and triples are longer, and they need extra space because they cannot be turned or stopped suddenly.

prompt: When managing space with a set of doubles, which is the right practice?
choices: Merge into small gaps because other drivers will make room
Change lanes quickly so you spend less time beside other vehicles
Keep the same following distance as a single trailer
Allow more following distance and wait for larger gaps before entering traffic
explanation: With doubles and triples, allow more following distance, make sure gaps are large enough before entering or crossing traffic, and be clear at the sides before changing lanes.

prompt: Why is there more chance of skids and loss of traction with doubles and triples in bad weather?
choices: The trailer brakes cannot be applied in rain
Converter dollies have no brakes
The drive axles must pull a longer rig with more dead axles
The trailers have smaller tires than single trailers
explanation: Doubles and triples have greater length and more dead axles to pull with the drive axles, so skids and loss of traction are more likely.

prompt: When parking doubles or triples, you should avoid:
choices: Lots with marked truck parking spaces
Spaces at the far end of a truck stop lot
Spots on firm, level pavement
A spot you cannot pull straight through
explanation: Do not get into a spot you cannot pull straight through. Know how the lot is arranged to avoid a long, difficult escape.

prompt: Converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have:
choices: Two air tanks
Spring brakes
Antilock brakes
A sliding fifth wheel
explanation: Converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, must have antilock brakes (ABS).

prompt: How can you tell that a converter dolly is equipped with antilock brakes?
choices: It has a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly
It has a blue tag on the pintle hook
It has a red lamp on the rear of the dolly
Its air tank petcock is painted yellow
explanation: Dollies with ABS have a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly.

prompt: You drive a 70-foot set of doubles at 55 mph. What is the minimum following distance the manual recommends?
choices: 7 seconds
8 seconds
6 seconds
4 seconds
explanation: Leave at least 1 second for each 10 feet of length (7 seconds for 70 feet), plus 1 more second above 40 mph, for 8 seconds total.

prompt: For the safest handling, where should the more heavily loaded trailer go in a set of doubles?
choices: In the rear position
Either position, as long as the dolly is under it
In the first position, right behind the tractor
It does not matter if both are under the weight limit
explanation: The more heavily loaded semitrailer should be first behind the tractor, with the lighter trailer at the rear.

prompt: You are coupling twin trailers. One holds 32,000 lb of cargo and the other 18,000 lb. Where does the 18,000-lb trailer go?
choices: In the rear position
Directly behind the tractor
Behind the tractor, if it is the longer trailer
In front, so the heavier load is pulled last
explanation: The lighter trailer belongs in the rear and the heavier one directly behind the tractor.

prompt: The second trailer has no spring brakes. Before coupling, how can you use the tractor to set its emergency brakes?
choices: Connect only the service line and press the brake pedal several times
Connect the emergency line, charge the tank, then disconnect the line
Connect both air lines and hold the trailer hand valve on fully
Open the trailer air tank petcock and let all the air drain out
explanation: Charging the trailer tank through the emergency line and then disconnecting it sets the trailer emergency brakes, if the slack adjusters are correctly adjusted.

prompt: When securing the second trailer before coupling, what should you do if you have any doubt about its brakes?
choices: Raise the landing gear
Drain the trailer air tank
Disconnect the light cord
Chock the wheels
explanation: Chock the wheels of the second trailer if you have any doubt about its brakes.

prompt: What is a converter dolly (converter gear)?
choices: A device that converts trailer spring brakes into air brakes
A small yard tractor used to move trailers around a terminal
A coupling device with one or two axles and a fifth wheel
A ramp that lets you load freight into the rear trailer
explanation: A converter gear on a dolly has one or two axles and a fifth wheel, letting a semitrailer be coupled to the rear of a tractor-trailer to form a double.

prompt: How do you release the brakes on a converter dolly that does not have spring brakes?
choices: Pull the dolly's pintle hook release
Push in the trailer air supply knob
Close the shut-off valves on the first trailer
Open the dolly's air tank petcock
explanation: Release dolly brakes by opening the air tank petcock. If the dolly has spring brakes, use the dolly parking brake control instead.

prompt: When you wheel the converter dolly into place in front of the second trailer, it should be lined up with:
choices: The second trailer's kingpin
The center of the tractor's fifth wheel
The rear bumper of the first trailer
The second trailer's landing gear
explanation: Move the dolly into position in front of the second trailer, in line with its kingpin.

prompt: After hooking the converter dolly to the front trailer, what should you do next?
choices: Lower the dolly support and drain the dolly air tank
Lock the pintle hook and raise the dolly support
Open the shut-off valves at the rear of the dolly
Connect the dolly air lines to the tractor glad hands
explanation: After hooking the dolly to the front trailer, lock the pintle hook and secure the converter gear support in the raised position.

prompt: Before backing the dolly under the rear trailer, how high should the trailer be?
choices: Slightly higher than the dolly's fifth wheel
Slightly lower than the center of the dolly's fifth wheel
High enough that the kingpin clears the fifth wheel
Exactly level with the top of the fifth wheel
explanation: The trailer must be slightly lower than the center of the fifth wheel, so the trailer is raised slightly when the dolly is pushed under.

prompt: Before backing the converter dolly under the rear trailer, you should make sure that:
choices: The trailer landing gear is already fully raised
The dolly air tank petcock is still open
The safety chains have already been connected
The trailer brakes are locked or the wheels chocked
explanation: Make sure the rear trailer's brakes are locked and/or its wheels are chocked before backing the dolly under it.

prompt: After backing the dolly under the rear trailer, why raise the landing gear slightly off the ground?
choices: To let the fifth wheel jaws close
To release the trailer brakes
To prevent damage if the trailer moves
To check the trailer height
explanation: Raise the landing gear slightly off the ground so it is not damaged if the trailer moves, then test the coupling.

prompt: How do you test the coupling between the converter dolly and the second trailer?
choices: Pull against the pin of the second semitrailer
Open the emergency line shut-off valve
Back up against the trailer at low speed
Press the brake pedal hard several times
explanation: Test the coupling by pulling against the pin of the second semitrailer, then make a visual check.

prompt: During a visual check of the dolly-to-trailer coupling, what should you see?
choices: Locking jaws left open until you complete the first turn
A small gap between the upper and lower fifth wheel for movement
The release arm pulled out to the unlocked position for turning
No gap between the fifth wheel plates and jaws closed on the kingpin
explanation: A correct coupling has no space between the upper and lower fifth wheel, with the locking jaws closed on the kingpin.

prompt: When inspecting the fifth wheel, where should the locking jaws be?
choices: Around the shank of the kingpin
Behind the kingpin, against the glide plate
Around the head of the kingpin
Just in front of the kingpin
explanation: The locking jaws must close around the shank, not the head, of the kingpin.

prompt: In a set of doubles, how should the shut-off valves at the rear of the first trailer be set?
choices: Closed on the service line, open on the emergency line
Half open
Open
Closed
explanation: Shut-off valves at the rear of front trailers must be open so air can reach the trailers behind them.

prompt: How should the shut-off valves at the rear of the last trailer be set?
choices: Open on the service line only
Closed
Open on the emergency line only
Open
explanation: The service and emergency shut-off valves at the rear of the last trailer must be closed, since no trailer is being towed behind it.

prompt: In a triples rig, how should the shut-off valves at the rear of the middle (second) trailer be set?
choices: Closed
Open
Open only while braking
Closed on the emergency line only
explanation: Every trailer that tows another trailer has its rear shut-offs open. Only the valves at the rear of the last trailer are closed.

prompt: During a doubles inspection, how should the converter dolly's air tank drain valve be set?
choices: Open only on the service side
Open
Closed
Partly open to drain moisture
explanation: The converter dolly air tank drain valve must be closed so the dolly holds air.

prompt: After coupling, you push in the air supply knob and open the emergency line shut-off at the rear of the second trailer. No air comes out. What does this mean?
choices: Something is wrong and the trailer brakes will not work
The trailers are coupled correctly and ready to go
The dolly has spring brakes, so no air is needed
The system is working because the valve should be closed
explanation: You should hear air at the rear of the second trailer. If air pressure isn't there, something is wrong and the brakes won't work.

prompt: Where should you park the rig before uncoupling the rear trailer?
choices: On a slight slope so the dolly rolls free
On any surface, as long as the wheels are chocked
At an angle so you can see the dolly in the mirror
In a straight line on firm, level ground
explanation: Park the rig in a straight line on firm, level ground and apply the parking brakes before uncoupling.

prompt: When uncoupling the rear trailer, why lower its landing gear before releasing the dolly?
choices: To close the dolly air tank
To take some weight off the dolly
To charge the trailer brakes
To lift the trailer off its kingpin
explanation: Lower the second trailer's landing gear enough to remove some weight from the dolly before pulling it out.

prompt: When uncoupling the rear trailer, what should you do before disconnecting the dolly's air lines?
choices: Open the shut-offs at the rear of the first semitrailer
Release the pintle hook
Push in the trailer air supply knob
Close the air shut-offs at the rear of the first semitrailer
explanation: Close the air shut-offs at the rear of the first semitrailer (and on the dolly if so equipped), then disconnect and secure the dolly lines.

prompt: Why must you never unlock the pintle hook while the dolly is still under the rear trailer?
choices: The rear trailer's spring brakes will release suddenly
The dolly air lines will be pulled apart and damaged
The tow bar may fly up and cause injury
The rear trailer's landing gear may collapse under load
explanation: Unlocking the pintle hook with the dolly under the rear trailer can make the tow bar fly up, possibly causing injury and making it very difficult to re-couple.

prompt: To pull the converter dolly out from under the rear trailer, you release the dolly's fifth wheel latch and then:
choices: Slowly pull the tractor, first trailer and dolly forward
Unlock the pintle hook and back the tractor away
Push the dolly out from under the trailer by hand
Raise the rear trailer's landing gear all the way up
explanation: After releasing the dolly fifth wheel latch, slowly pull the tractor, first semitrailer and dolly forward to pull the dolly out.

prompt: The dolly has been pulled out from under the rear trailer. What should you do before releasing the pintle hook?
choices: Open the dolly air tank petcock but leave the safety chains attached
Reconnect the dolly air lines so its brakes stay applied while parked
Release the pintle hook first, then lower the dolly landing gear afterward
Lower its landing gear, unhook the chains, and set its brakes or chock it
explanation: To uncouple the dolly: lower its landing gear, disconnect the safety chains, apply its spring brakes or chock its wheels, then release the pintle hook and pull clear slowly.

prompt: When uncoupling a triple-trailer rig, which trailer do you uncouple first?
choices: The third (last) trailer
The second trailer
Any trailer, as long as the rig is straight
The first trailer
explanation: Uncouple the third trailer first by pulling the dolly out and unhitching it, then uncouple the rest like a double.

prompt: How should you couple and uncouple a less common truck-trailer combination?
choices: Use whatever method gets the job done fastest
Follow the manufacturer's and/or owner's specifications
Ask another driver on the road
Use the same steps as for triples in every case
explanation: There are too many combinations to cover in the manual. Learn the correct method from the manufacturer and/or owner specifications.

prompt: What inspection procedure should you use for a doubles or triples combination?
choices: A quick walk-around of the last trailer
Only a check of the coupling devices
The seven-step inspection procedure, plus the added combination checks
The same check used for a single straight truck, nothing more
explanation: Use the seven-step inspection procedure from Section 2, plus the additional checks for coupling systems, dollies and shut-off valves.

prompt: When checking a sliding fifth wheel, what position problem should you look for?
choices: Positioned so the locking pins can be seen from the side of the rig
Centered over the tractor's drive axles with all pins locked
So far back that the trailer kingpin cannot reach the locking jaws
So far forward that the tractor hits the landing gear or trailer in turns
explanation: Make sure the sliding fifth wheel is not so far forward that the tractor frame will hit the landing gear, or the cab will hit the trailer, during turns.

prompt: How should the air lines to the trailers be secured?
choices: Tied to the safety chains
With enough slack for turns and no air leaks
Pulled tight so they cannot drag
Taped to the light cords at each glad hand
explanation: Air lines must be properly connected to the glad hands, free of leaks and damage, and secured with enough slack for turns.

prompt: When inspecting the landing gear of a trailer you are about to pull, it should be:
choices: Lowered slightly so it can help support the trailer
Removed from its mount, with the crank handle stowed in the cab
Fully raised, with the crank handle secured
Raised only halfway so you can park more quickly
explanation: Landing gear must be fully raised, undamaged, with the crank handle in place and secured.

prompt: During a doubles inspection, what should you check at the pintle hook?
choices: The pintle eye is in the hook and the hook is latched
The safety chains are removed so they cannot drag
The hook is freshly greased and left in the open position
The hook is left unlatched so the dolly can swivel freely
explanation: Be sure the dolly's pintle eye is in the pintle hook, the hook is latched, and the safety chains are secured.

prompt: Before checking that air flows to all trailers, how should you hold the vehicle in place?
choices: Hold the brake pedal down
Leave it in gear with the engine idling
Use the trailer hand valve
Use the tractor parking brake and/or chock the wheels
explanation: Use the tractor parking brake and/or chock the wheels, and wait for normal air pressure before the test.

prompt: During the air-flow check on doubles, where do you open the emergency line shut-off valve?
choices: At the rear of the first trailer
On the converter dolly air tank
At the rear of the last trailer
At the tractor glad hands
explanation: Open the emergency line shut-off at the rear of the last trailer. Escaping air shows the entire system is charged.

prompt: During the air-flow check you hear no air at the rear of the last trailer. What should you check first?
choices: That the shut-off valves on the trailers and dollies are open
That the dolly air tank petcock is open
That the trailer spring brakes are applied
That the tractor protection valve has popped out
explanation: If you don't hear air escaping from both lines, check that the shut-off valves on the trailers and dollies are in the OPEN position.

prompt: To confirm service air reaches the back of a doubles rig, you open the service line valve at the rear. This test works only if:
choices: The trailer air supply knob is pulled out
The trailer hand brake or service brake pedal is applied
The dolly's spring brakes are released by hand
The engine is off and the tanks are drained
explanation: The service line only carries air when the brakes are applied, so the test assumes the trailer handbrake or service brake pedal is on.

prompt: When testing the tractor protection valve, at about what pressure should the trailer air supply knob pop out?
choices: Usually between 60 and 80 psi
Usually between 20 and 45 psi
Only when pressure reaches 0 psi
Usually between 100 and 125 psi
explanation: As you pump the air down, the trailer air supply control should pop out in the range set by the manufacturer, usually 20 to 45 psi.

prompt: Why is a working tractor protection valve important on a doubles rig?
choices: It controls the converter dolly's antilock brakes
It keeps the trailer brakes released if air is lost
It stops the trailers from rolling forward when parked
Without it, a hose or trailer brake leak could drain all the tractor's air
explanation: If the tractor protection valve fails, a hose or trailer brake leak could drain the tractor's air, setting the emergency brakes and possibly causing loss of control.

prompt: How do you test the trailer emergency brakes?
choices: Pull out the air supply control and tug gently on the trailer
Apply the hand valve hard while driving at highway speed
Pump the brake pedal until the low air warning signal comes on
Disconnect the service line while moving forward slowly
explanation: After checking that the trailer rolls freely, stop, pull out the trailer air supply control, and pull gently to confirm the trailer emergency brakes are on.

prompt: The trailer service brakes should be tested with the hand valve. How should they be controlled in normal driving?
choices: With the trailer air supply knob
With the tractor parking brake control
With the foot brake pedal
With the hand valve (trolley valve)
explanation: Test trailer brakes with the hand valve, but in normal driving use the foot pedal, which applies the service brakes at all wheels.

prompt: Why should you chock a converter dolly or trailer without spring brakes when you park it?
choices: Its pintle hook can unlatch on a slope
Its emergency brakes hold only while air remains in its tank
Federal rules forbid setting its emergency brakes
Its brakes release when the light cord is unplugged
explanation: Dollies and trailers without spring brakes rely on air in the trailer tank. When that air leaks away there are no brakes, so use wheel chocks.
